item.title: Lima
item.description:
Lima is devvm’s backend, so every new VM runs on it (a VM’s backend). Each project gets a full VM with a kernel of its own, which runs on Apple’s Virtualization framework (vz) on macOS and on QEMU on Linux. How it works › Lima explains how devvm sets up, confines and clones Lima’s VMs.

Requirements

  • macOS 13 or newer, on arm64 or x86_64.
  • Lima 2.2 or newer, with limactl on your PATH. Install it with Homebrew, brew install lima, or see Lima’s install guide.
  • Linux on arm64 or x86_64.
  • Lima 2.2 or newer, with limactl on your PATH. Install it with Homebrew, brew install lima, or see Lima’s install guide.
  • QEMU from your package manager: qemu-system-aarch64 (or qemu-system-x86_64) and qemu-img.
  • Read and write access to /dev/kvm. That means virtualization is turned on in the firmware (or nested virtualization, in a VM), and your user is in the kvm group.

Every command that needs Lima checks these first and stops at the first one that’s missing. devvm doctor lists them all, each with the command that installs it where there’s one to run. That’s Homebrew’s command for Lima when you have Homebrew, your package manager’s for QEMU (apt, dnf, pacman or zypper), and sudo usermod -aG kvm $USER for /dev/kvm, after which you log in again. devvm never runs them itself (details).

devvm’s Lima home

devvm keeps its VMs and images in a Lima home of its own, ~/.local/share/devvm/lima (under $XDG_DATA_HOME when that’s set), whatever LIMA_HOME says. Your own Lima VMs stay where they are, and Lima settings you made for them don’t reach devvm’s VMs. Because of this, a plain limactl list doesn’t show devvm’s VMs, so run devvm limactl list instead (below). To keep devvm’s VMs somewhere else, such as a sandbox or a shorter path, set DEVVM_LIMA_HOME to that folder.

Lima adds _config/default.yaml and _config/override.yaml from its home to every VM it starts, so devvm refuses to start a VM while devvm’s Lima home holds either file, and you move them out of it to go on. devvm also refuses a VM that has a network devvm didn’t give it, because a second network would get around the VM’s proxy, so remove the networks: entries from the file that devvm names (why).

Running limactl

devvm limactl ARGS... runs limactl with ARGS on devvm’s Lima home, in devvm’s place. Its input, output, terminal and exit code are limactl’s, and devvm passes every option on to it, --help included. devvm help limactl shows devvm’s own help for the command.

devvm limactl list
devvm limactl shell --start devvm-img-<key>
  • It runs from devvm’s data folder, as devvm’s own limactl commands do, so give files by their absolute path.
  • It runs without your SSH agent, so a VM never gets your agent through it, whatever its SSH agent choice says (why).
  • A VM you start this way, with devvm limactl start or shell --start, runs unconfined, whatever its tier, and devvm ls shows it as unenforced (confinement). Start project VMs with devvm.

File watchers

A dev server or a watcher that runs in the VM, such as Vite, webpack, tsc --watch or nodemon, learns about changed files from the VM’s kernel. The kernel sees every change made in the VM, so a file that a coding agent or a command in the VM’s shell writes reaches the watcher at once. Lima’s mounts don’t pass on the changes you make on this machine, though, so a watcher in the VM misses a file you save in your editor here, and the dev server doesn’t reload. On Linux the project folder is a 9p mount, and there a watcher also misses the VM’s own changes in the folder’s subfolders, and sees only those to files at the top of the folder.

To have a watcher see your edits, set it to poll the project folder, which costs some CPU in a large project:

Tool Setting
chokidar, and tools built on it CHOKIDAR_USEPOLLING=1
Vite server.watch.usePolling: true in vite.config
webpack watchOptions.poll in webpack.config.js, or WATCHPACK_POLLING=true
nodemon nodemon --legacy-watch
tsc --watch "watchOptions": { "watchFile": "fixedPollingInterval" } in tsconfig.json
cargo watch cargo watch --poll

Set the variables in the VM’s shell or in your project’s scripts, before the tool starts. Leave Lima’s own file event setting, mountInotify, off, because with it on, commands in the VM that write to the project folder, such as git init, fail at random (details).

Cleaning up

devvm gc deletes devvm’s stale and unfinished Lima images and the shared tools that no VM has and that aren’t current, and it leaves your VMs as they are. devvm images rm deletes an image that’s current, except on Linux hosts one whose disk VMs use (cleaning up). Lima also keeps a download cache of its own, which holds Ubuntu’s cloud images that devvm’s builds downloaded, and which your own Lima VMs share. devvm gc --caches deletes the cloud images that devvm downloads and that no image of devvm’s names, after listing them and asking, and devvm never runs limactl prune, which empties the whole cache (what devvm keeps).

Limits

  • Folder names in VM names are cut short. Lima keeps each VM’s ssh socket in the VM’s folder in its home, and a socket path has fewer than 104 characters. A long Lima home leaves less room for the name, so set DEVVM_LIMA_HOME to a shorter folder if devvm says the home is too long, or that a VM’s name leaves no room for the folder’s name (VM names).
  • Paths can’t contain commas. Lima and QEMU split mount options on commas, so devvm refuses to mount a project folder whose path has one, and it leaves out an agent’s folder whose path has one, with a warning.
  • Disks can grow but not shrink.
  • Mounts on Linux are 9p. A 9p share mounts once per guest, and file watchers in the VM miss changes in its subfolders (file watchers).
  • A VM that Lima reports as failed to start still starts, with a warning, when it’s running but degraded because one of Lima’s boot scripts failed. A VM that doesn’t answer over ssh within a minute is stopped instead, and its console log is in its Lima folder (serial*.log).
